title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Scheduling, Profiling & Ops Playbook (Team Wiki)
author: Ava Chen
content:
Overview

This page consolidates the serving runtime documentation, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, kernel scheduling guidance, operational runbooks, known issues, and team wiki notes. It is intended as the canonical reference for engineers who operate, profile, and extend the Redwood serving runtime. Use the links in Related Pages for detailed reference docs and release-specific notes.

Goals
- Provide a concise architecture summary that explains core runtime components and dataflows.
- Capture kernel scheduling policies and tuning knobs used in production.
- Document a step-by-step profiling playbook for diagnosing performance regressions.
- Describe the standardized benchmarking suite and baseline metrics we run for each release.
- Maintain operational runbooks for common incidents (latency spikes, OOMs, degraded throughput).
- Record known issues and short-term mitigations until permanent fixes are merged.

Audience and Ownership
- Primary audience: serving runtime engineers, SREs, and platform owners responsible for inference performance.
- Oncall contact: serving-runtime-team@redwood.ai (pager handled via PagerDuty).
- Documentation owner: Serving Runtime team (eng owner).

1) Runtime architecture (high level)

Summary: The runtime is a modular, GPU-optimized inference engine with a control plane that manages model variants, routing, and autoscaling. The runtime emphasizes three capabilities: low-latency single-stream inference, high-throughput batching, and KV cache-aware continuation for chat-style workloads.

Core components:
- Frontend API gateway: validates requests, attaches metadata (customer, route, model pin), and enforces quotas.
- Router & policy engine: implements routing policies (latency-first, cost-first, region affinity) and selects an execution target (hosted Pool / Dedicated / Private).
- Scheduler: maps logical requests to physical execution slots and assigns kernel launch plans (see Kernel scheduling).
- Execution worker (per-GPU): manages model shards/placements, KV caches, per-request KV lookups, batching queues, and kernel orchestration.
- Batcher: continuous batching queue with adaptive batch-size decisions driven by latency SLOs and traffic shape.
- Cache layer: prefix/KV cache for prompt reuse and short-circuiting repeated compute.
- Telemetry & tracing: token-level latency, GPU utilization, queueing, and kernel timing exported to Prometheus/Grafana and Perfetto traces.

Data flow (request lifecycle):
1. Ingress request hits API gateway -> auth & quota checks.
2. Router applies policy and maps to an execution pool.
3. Scheduler decides between immediate single-stream execution or enqueue for batching.
4. Batcher batches requests then dispatches kernels to Execution worker.
5. Worker performs kernel launches, updates KV cache, streams tokens back via the gateway.

SLOs (production baseline):
- Latency SLO (interactive models): 95th percentile <= 150ms for <128 token responses under steady-state.
- Throughput SLO (batch optimized): target > 1.8K tokens/s per A100-40GB equivalent under sustained batched workload.
- Error budget: <0.1% 5xx errors per 24h window.

2) Kernel scheduling: policies and knobs

Overview: Kernel scheduling decides which CUDA/cuBLAS/cuDNN/TVM kernels run, when to preempt, and how to multiplex GPU resources across concurrent requests. The scheduler implements two high-level modes: Latency-first and Throughput-first. Engineers can annotate model variants with preferred scheduling profiles.

Scheduling modes and tradeoffs:
- Latency-first
  - Prioritizes single-request tail-latency.
  - Uses preemptible small-batch kernel launches with prioritized streams.
  - Lower GPU efficiency due to smaller batch sizes; used for interactive, low-concurrency routes.
- Throughput-first
  - Maximizes GPU utilization via large-batch aggregation, deferred kernel launches, and cooperative multi-request packing.
  - Higher throughput and lower cost per token, higher tail-latency under bursty traffic.

Key knobs (runtime flags and config fields):
- schedule.mode: "latency" | "throughput" (per-route override).
- batch.max_size: integer (max tokens per batch).
- batch.max_wait_ms: integer (ms to wait before dispatching an unfinished batch).
- preempt.enabled: boolean (allow priority preemption).
- stream.priority_threshold: integer (requests with priority >= threshold get dedicated high-priority CUDA streams).
- cache.prefetch_k: integer (number of KV entries to prefetch for continuation requests).
- kernel.alpha_pack_factor: float (controls how aggressively kernels will pack multiple requests into fused kernels).

Best practices:
- For interactive chat endpoints: set schedule.mode=latency, batch.max_size=8, batch.max_wait_ms=6.
- For batch embedding pipelines: set schedule.mode=throughput, batch.max_size>=256, batch.max_wait_ms>=50.
- Avoid enabling aggressive kernel.alpha_pack_factor on models with highly variable sequence lengths; it can increase tail-latency.

3) Profiling playbook (step-by-step)

When to run: any unexplained regression in latency, throughput, or error-rate compared to the last known-good baseline.

Telemetry to check first (5 minute triage):
1. Dashboards: route-level latency P50/P95/P99, queue depth, batch size distribution.
2. GPU metrics: p99 SM utilization, GPU mem utilization, ECC errors, GPU temperature.
3. Logs: worker stderr, kernel launch latencies, OOM traces (OOM stack).
4. Recent deploys: check rollout timeline and model changes.

Profiling steps (detailed):
1. Reproduce in staging: replay a production trace (use the trace-replay harness in bench-suite).
2. Capture a Perfetto trace on the execution worker during the repro (10–30s window).
   - Command: perfettoctl record --output=/tmp/trace.pb --duration=30 --categories=gpu,kernel,ipc
3. Run nvprof or Nsight Systems for kernel-level timings if Perfetto indicates kernel spikes.
   - Example: nsight-sys --trace-level=nvtx --output=nsys-report.qdrep --duration=20 --target-pid <worker-pid>
4. Inspect trace for: kernel launch time distribution, stream contention, long host-side stalls, memcpy staging times, and batch aggregation errors.
5. Check memory allocator fragmentation: enable tcmalloc / mallinfo dumps to verify fragmentation.
6. Toggle scheduling knobs in a staging canary and re-run the workload to measure impact.

Remediation checklist (common fixes):
- If high queue depth + small batches: reduce batch.max_wait_ms or enable preempt for latency routes.
- If long memcpy or host stalls: move to pinned memory buffers and enable async memcpy.
- If kernel contention on specific ops (e.g., flash attention): try alternative fused kernel or increase per-kernel stream parallelism.
- If fragmentation / frequent OOMs: enable workspace growth policy or restart worker with defragmentation script.

4) Benchmarking suite: design and standard runs

Purpose: The bench-suite provides reproducible, CI-driven benchmarks for latency, throughput, and cost metrics across model families and hardware profiles. Results are stored in the benchmark database and used to gate releases.

Workloads included:
- Interactive chat synthetic traces (mix of short and long prompts).
- Steady-state batch-token generation (embedding/LLM scoring).
- KV-cache continuation workloads for chat sessions (high prefix reuse).
- Multi-tenant packing scenarios to measure fairness and isolation.

Standard metrics we capture:
- Token/sec (sustained) and tokens/cost-dollar.
- P50/P95/P99 latencies for end-to-end response.
- Batch size distribution and % requests in single-shot path.
- GPU SM utilization, achieved TFLOPS for major ops.
- Memory high-water marks and fragmentation ratio.

CI integration and release gating:
- Each runtime PR must run the bench-suite against the latest mainline model artifacts on an isolated benchmark cluster.
- Regressions: any >5% regression in P95 latency or >7% regression in tokens/sec relative to baseline requires an ADR or revert.

How to run locally (example):
- Checkout bench-suite: git clone git@repo:redwood/bench-suite.git
- Run interactive profile: ./bench-suite/run.sh --profile interactive --model gptx-3-small --hardware a100-40
- Results will be published to bench-db and a permalink will be printed in stdout.

5) Release notes (summary for recent release)

Version v1.24.0 (released 2026-06-10)
- Improvements:
  - New adaptive batcher algorithm that reduces P95 latency by ~8% on interactive routes (config flag: batch.adaptive=true).
  - Kernel fusion update for flash-attention v2: improved throughput for long sequences (+12% tokens/s).
- Fixes:
  - Resolved intermittent GPU allocator OOM caused by temporary workspace overcommit during multi-tenant packing.
  - Fixed a race in cache invalidation that could return stale KV entries across rollouts.
- Known impact: Canary rollout showed a 1–2% increase in 99th percentile latency for a small subset of routes; mitigation flag batch.alpha_pack_factor default reduced to 0.6.

6) Known issues and short-term mitigations

ID: KI-2026-045 - Intermittent long-tail latency on multi-tenant packing
- Symptoms: P99 latency spikes correlated with high variance in sequence length.
- Root cause: aggressive packing fused kernels cause head-of-line blocking.
- Mitigation: set batch.alpha_pack_factor=0.5 for affected pools and enable per-request max_seq_length cap.
- Owner: Diego Ramirez.

ID: KI-2026-052 - Occasional GPU OOM during rolling upgrades
- Symptoms: OOM logs on worker during model swap; worker crashes and auto-restarts.
- Mitigation: enable staggered model swap (upgrade.stagger_count=3) and pre-warm workspace before draining (prewarm.workspace=true).
- Owner: Priya Nair.

ID: KI-2026-061 - NVLINK saturation during cross-GPU KV sync
- Symptoms: elevated PCIe/NVLINK latency and reduced memcpy throughput.
- Mitigation: throttle sync frequency (kv.sync_interval_ms=200) and schedule KV syncs to low-traffic windows.
- Owner: Samir Patel.

7) Runtime runbooks (operational)

A) Latency spike (interactive route)
1. Triage: check route dashboard for P95/P99, queue depth, batch size distribution.
2. If queue depth > threshold and batch sizes are small: reduce batch.max_wait_ms or set route to schedule.mode=latency.
3. If kernel launch delays present: collect Perfetto trace and escalate to runtime-oncall with trace link.
4. If persistent after config toggles: failover traffic to fallback model variant (router policy: fallback-to=smaller-model-latency) and open incident.
5. Postmortem: run profiling playbook, attach traces, and create regression ticket if caused by recent deploy.

B) GPU OOM on worker
1. Identify worker and affected model via error logs.
2. Check memory high-water mark in metrics and compare to model memory profile.
3. If fragmentation suspected: restart worker with defrag script (command: /opt/runtime/bin/defrag-worker --graceful).
4. If persistent on model swap: enable upgrade.stagger_count and prewarm workspace.
5. Notify customer-facing teams if customer traffic impacted.

C) Degraded throughput under batch workloads
1. Check batch size distribution and batch.max_size.
2. If batch sizes are small due to batch.max_wait_ms: increase max_wait_ms in staging and run bench-suite.
3. If SM utilization low: validate kernel fusion version and consider disabling a new fused kernel as a canary.

8) Team wiki and operational notes

Oncall rotations and eskalation:
- Primary oncall: Serving Runtime SRE rotation (weekly).
- Escalation: if issue not resolved in 30 minutes, escalate to Runtime Lead (pager) and open a Sev ticket.

Useful links and dashboards:
- Grafana: runtime/overview (P50/P95/P99, GPU utilization)
- Bench DB: bench-suite/latest (historical benchmark runs)
- Perfetto traces: perfetto/trace-store (search by trace id printed in logs)
- Runbook index: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/serving-runtime-runbooks-and-playbook-2026.json

Onboarding checklist for new runtime engineers:
1. Read this page and the runtime reference architecture doc.
2. Run the bench-suite locally against a baseline model.
3. Shadow oncall for 2 weeks with a senior engineer.
4. Complete the profiling playbook exercise and submit a short write-up.

Appendix: common CLI snippets and examples
- Start a perfetto capture on a worker (staging):
  perfettoctl record --output=/tmp/trace.pb --duration=30 --categories=gpu,kernel,ipc

- Run bench-suite interactive profile:
  ./bench-suite/run.sh --profile interactive --model gptx-3-small --hardware a100-40

- Restart a single worker gracefully:
  /opt/runtime/bin/workerctl restart --worker-id <id> --graceful

- Toggle route to latency mode (example API):
  curl -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' -d '{"route":"chat-prod","config":{"schedule.mode":"latency","batch.max_wait_ms":6}}' https://admin-api.internal.redwood/v1/routes/update

Document maintenance
- This page should be reviewed quarterly or after any major runtime release.
- Reviewer rotation: Diego Ramirez (performance), Priya Nair (ops), Samir Patel (kernel).

If you find inconsistencies or missing runbooks, file a documentation PR against this page or ping the runtime-docs channel.
